# Agent Skills

A catalogue of reusable **Agent Skills** and orchestrating agent definitions for
software engineering, learning, workflow improvement, and accountable
AI-assisted delivery.

Skills are portable procedure packages. Agents coordinate skills, lifecycle,
state, delegation, and human responsibility boundaries.

## Repository structure

```text
agents/
  <agent-name>.md          # orchestration and workflow state

<skill-name>/
  SKILL.md                 # canonical Agent Skills entry point
  references/              # optional, loaded on demand
  scripts/                 # optional deterministic helpers
  assets/                  # optional output resources
```

## Packaging rules

Every skill is self-contained and can be installed by copying its own directory.

- The entry point is `<skill-name>/SKILL.md`.
- Supporting files live inside that skill's directory.
- A skill must not depend on a repository-level shared folder, parent path,
  another skill's directory, or an agent definition.
- Small process guidance may be duplicated when that preserves portability.
- Relative references should be direct from `SKILL.md`; avoid nested reference
  chains.
- Keep active `SKILL.md` instructions under 500 lines. Move optional detail into
  focused references.

Canonical frontmatter uses only specification fields:

```yaml
---
name: skill-name
description: What the skill does and when to use it.
license: Apache-2.0                # optional
compatibility: Requires git ...   # optional
metadata:                         # optional string mapping
  example.key: "value"
allowed-tools: Bash(git:*) Read   # optional, experimental
---
```

Runtime-specific properties must not be added as new top-level fields to the
canonical skill. Store portable extension information under namespaced
`metadata`, then translate it into a generated harness adapter when needed.

## Agent workflow artefacts

Repository-local supporting artefacts created by agents or skills use one
canonical root:

```text
.agent-artifacts/<work-branch>/<workflow>/<artifact>
```

Use the exact short work-branch name and preserve `/` as path separators. For
example, artefacts for `feature/PAY-1234` live under
`.agent-artifacts/feature/PAY-1234/`. A PR-scoped workflow uses the PR head
branch; a working-tree workflow uses the active branch. When no named branch can
be resolved for a revision-bound operation, use
`.agent-artifacts/detached/<full-head-sha>/...`.

Revision-sensitive workflows should add a revision directory beneath the
workflow when one is available, for example:

```text
.agent-artifacts/feature/PAY-1234/review/<head-sha>/report.md
.agent-artifacts/feature/PAY-1234/review/<head-sha>/risk-map.json
.agent-artifacts/feature/PAY-1234/implement/<commit-sha>/implementation-evidence.json
.agent-artifacts/feature/PAY-1234/create-pr/<head-sha>/body.md
```

For an uncommitted working-tree review, use a clearly non-revision label such as
`review/working-tree/` and bind the artefact content to the reviewed base plus
working-tree evidence or digest.

This root is intentionally suitable for a single `.gitignore` entry. Before
writing repository-local supporting artefacts, verify the root is ignored and
contains no tracked files. Never add or modify ignore rules implicitly. If the
canonical root is not safely ignored, return the artefact inline or keep it in
orchestration state when possible; if an on-disk artefact is required to
continue, stop with the missing storage prerequisite rather than writing to an
arbitrary repository path or external temporary directory.

The convention applies to workflow-supporting outputs such as review reports,
risk maps, implementation-evidence packets, resumable checkpoints, generated
handoffs, and temporary PR bodies. It does not relocate user-requested product
or repository deliverables that are meant to be tracked as part of the change.

## Public and internal skills

Public skills may be invoked directly. Workflow-internal modules sit behind an
agent interface and fail closed without the owning agent's orchestration state.

Internal modules use canonical metadata such as:

```yaml
metadata:
  mhingston.internal: "true"
  mhingston.owner-agent: "pr-review"
  mhingston.user-invocable: "false"
```

This metadata communicates intent but is not an authorization boundary. The
module's body must still require its owning agent's exact context and return
`REQUIRED_ORCHESTRATOR_CONTEXT` when invoked directly. A runtime adapter may map
the metadata to its native visibility mechanism.

## Agent catalogue

| Agent | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| [`implement`](agents/implement.md) | Orchestrate a ready ticket through a ticket-keyed feature branch, delegated behaviour-first implementation with falsifiable verification, independent technical review, explicit contract reconciliation, full build/test gates, and pull-request creation. |
| [`pr-review`](agents/pr-review.md) | Require a current independent technical review and revision-bound risk map, provide proportionate comprehension support, redirect unresolved architecture decisions upstream, prepare explicit human judgement, and record the human verdict without approving or merging. |
| [`refine`](agents/refine.md) | Classify selected work, clarify unresolved decisions, refine one bounded ticket or split larger clear work into agent-ready vertical slices, resolve publication targets, and update the selected tracker after human approval. |

## Suggested workflows

The catalogue is composable rather than one mandatory SDLC. Start with the
smallest workflow that owns the outcome; add adjacent skills only when their
extra evidence or control is useful. Square brackets below indicate optional
stages rather than required ceremony.

| Goal | Suggested flow | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deliver a ticket | `refine` → [`plan`] → `implement` → [`pr-review`] | `plan` is useful when design or uncertainty deserves a separate non-mutating pass. `implement` already owns implementation, independent technical review, contract reconciliation, final project gates, and `create-pr`. Add `pr-review` when the formal human-verdict lifecycle is required. |
| Isolate an unclear bug or regression | `fault-isolation` → [`plan`] → `implement` | Use `fault-isolation` when the causal mechanism is not established. Hand off the supported root cause, minimised reproducer, and candidate regression oracle; skip the diagnostic stage when the defect and oracle are already known. |
| Reconcile a conflicted Git integration | `integration-reconciliation` | Standalone flow for an active merge, rebase, or cherry-pick. It reconstructs both sides' intent, preserves compatible behaviour, validates the integrated state, and blocks rather than inventing a product decision when authority is unresolved. |
| Adopt coding agents in a repository | `agent-readiness` → targeted remediation → reassess | Route gaps to the owning capability such as `project-context`, `repository-ontology`, `agent-observability`, or `agent-workflow-design`; readiness itself remains an assessment, not a remediation workflow. |
| Reduce coding-convention drift | `code-conventions` → targeted codification → CI verification | Mine explicit and implicit conventions, choose only objective high-value rules, extend the existing formatter/linter/analyzer stack, and roll out with baselines or no-new-violations where legacy debt is material. |
| Design an agent system | `agent-readiness` → `agent-workflow-design` → `agent-observability` | Add `programmatic-tool-calling` for bounded multi-tool loops. Use `dynamic-workflows` when Mastra is specifically the executable runtime. |
| Improve skills from experience | `wrap-up` → `session-lessons` → `skill-creator` | One run produces observations; longitudinal evidence qualifies durable changes; `skill-creator` evaluates proposed revisions. A validated escaped defect may seed regression evaluation early but does not bypass the codification gate. |
| Adopt an external practice | `adopt` → existing owning skill or agent → `skill-creator` evaluation | Prefer strengthening the existing responsibility over adding a parallel workflow. Use a new skill only when the source reveals a genuinely distinct reusable contract. |
| Maintain durable project context | `project-context` + `decision-continuity` + [`repository-ontology`] | `project-context` owns the durable substrate, `decision-continuity` protects attributable accepted direction, and ontology is optional when semantic traversal or validation earns its cost. |
| Maintain shared organisational memory | `memory-recall` → work → `memory-capture` → periodic `memory-maintenance` | Shared memory complements project context and canonical sources; it does not automatically become authoritative over them. |
| Review and improve review | `review` or `pr-review` → accumulated revision-bound evidence → `review-calibration` | Use `review` for standalone technical review, `pr-review` for the orchestrated PR/human-verdict lifecycle, and `review-calibration` for evidence-backed changes to review policy. |
| Execute quality-sensitive parallel work | accepted plan/specification → `gauntlet-loop` | Use when dependency-aware fan-out plus independent adversarial verification earns its overhead. It does not replace planning, source authority, or human decisions. |

## Choosing related skills

Several skills are deliberately adjacent without being substitutes for each
other:

| If you need to... | Use | Rather than |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decide how much coding-agent autonomy an environment can safely support | `agent-readiness` | using `agent-workflow-design` as a maturity assessment |
| Design the workflow/state machine around agents | `agent-workflow-design` | treating `agent-readiness` as an implementation design |
| Make an agent workflow reconstructable from traces and receipts | `agent-observability` | treating observability as correctness or approval |
| Implement a Mastra-owned executable workflow | `dynamic-workflows` | using it for runtime-neutral workflow design |
| Optimize a bounded repeated multi-tool stage | `programmatic-tool-calling` | building a full workflow runtime around one loop |
| Discover project coding norms and turn objective ones into deterministic checks | `code-conventions` | using `review` as a style-mining workflow or treating code prevalence as policy |
| Configure repository language-server wiring | `lsp-config` | using convention discovery to manage editor/LSP integration |
| Establish durable project truth/intent/history/scratch relationships | `project-context` | turning shared memory or an ontology into a second source of truth |
| Model repository entities and semantic relationships | `repository-ontology` | using ontology machinery for ordinary project documentation |
| Preserve accepted/rejected/deferred direction across resumed work | `decision-continuity` | reconstructing intent from implementation or chat history |
| Isolate why a concrete bug, regression, flake, or slowdown is happening | `fault-isolation` | using `code-research` for a reported failure or jumping straight to implementation from a plausible theory |
| Establish uncertain runtime/library/compatibility semantics with a controlled experiment | `code-research` | inventing a concrete failure just to fit `fault-isolation` |
| Reconcile an active merge/rebase/cherry-pick conflict from both sides' intent | `integration-reconciliation` | using generic `decision-continuity` or code review to edit conflict markers |
| Retrieve or persist reusable shared organisational knowledge | `memory-recall` / `memory-capture` | treating shared memory as canonical project state |
| Review one concrete change | `review` | using historical `review-calibration` as a reviewer |
| Run the full PR evidence and human-verdict lifecycle | `pr-review` | expecting standalone `review` to approve or merge |
| Improve review dimensions, thresholds, or routing from historical evidence | `review-calibration` | silently changing review policy inside a single review |
| Capture useful evidence from one ending session | `wrap-up` | promoting a one-off observation directly into durable guidance |
| Find recurring patterns across sessions and PR lifecycles | `session-lessons` | using one session as proof of a general rule |
| Create or revise a reusable skill and measure its effect | `skill-creator` | treating a lesson or incident as an automatic skill change |

## Responsibility boundaries

1. Evidence is not approval.
2. Explanation is not proof of correctness.
3. Technical severity is not policy disposition.
4. A policy threshold is not a human verdict.
5. Model-generated rationale or risk acceptance is not human judgement.
6. A review artefact or verdict applies only to the exact revision it names.
7. Green checks cannot silently replace explicit risk acceptance.
8. Automation may enforce a recorded verdict but must not invent one.
9. Agents coordinate capabilities; they do not erase responsibility boundaries.
10. Portability and correct skill-loading boundaries take priority over avoiding
    small amounts of duplicated guidance.

## Validation

Validation has two distinct layers. A green result in one layer must not be
reported as evidence from the other.

### Static and deterministic validation

The repository validates every top-level skill on pushes and pull requests using
the official `skills-ref` validator pinned to a reviewed upstream commit. It also
enforces the repository's 500-line active-instruction policy and runs bundled
deterministic script tests. These checks establish package, format, and helper-tool
integrity; they do **not** establish that a changed skill improves agent behaviour.

Local validation:

```bash
python -m pip install \
  "git+https://github.com/agentskills/agentskills.git@38a2ff82958afee88dadf4831509e6f7e9d8ef4e#subdirectory=skills-ref"
for skill_md in */SKILL.md; do
  skills-ref validate "$(dirname "$skill_md")"
done

python3 skill-creator/scripts/test-aggregate-evals.py
python3 contributor-analysis/scripts/test-analyse-contributors.py
python3 git-archaeologist/scripts/test-analyse-history.py
node --test lsp-config/scripts/detect-languages.test.mjs
python3 repository-ontology/scripts/test-ontology-guard.py
python3 project-context/scripts/test-validate-context-record.py
python3 wrap-up/scripts/test-wrap-up-hooks.py
node teach-me/scripts/learning-state.test.mjs
node teach-me/scripts/learning-engine.test.mjs
```

### Behavioural evaluation

When a material skill change can be executed in a real deployment or reference
harness, compare the candidate with the exact base-revision skill package under
matched prompts, fixtures, model, harness, permissions, tools, and verifier.
Behavioural evaluation is additional evidence, not a reinterpretation of static
CI. If the required harness, credentials, baseline, or verifier is unavailable,
report the behavioural result as `NOT_RUN` or `BLOCKED` rather than treating green
static validation as a behavioural pass.

See [`skill-creator`](skill-creator/SKILL.md) and
[`skill-creator/references/ci-evaluation.md`](skill-creator/references/ci-evaluation.md)
for the evaluation and CI contracts.

## Installation

Copy each required public skill directory into the location used by the target
agent harness. Install canonical agent definitions from `agents/` separately and
adapt them to the harness's agent format.

When a harness supports generated adapters, translate namespaced metadata there;

Do not use for planning one ordinary repository change or assessing whether an existing repository is ready for agents.\n---\n\n# Design Agent Workflows\n\nDesign agentic systems as explicit workflows whose correctness does not depend on\nconversation memory, model self-report, or prompt compliance alone. Classify every phase before choosing agents\n\nFor each candidate phase ask: **why does this require a model?** Classify it as\none of:\n\n| Kind | Use when | Typical owner |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `human` | accountable judgement, approval, clarification, or system input is required | named person or role |\n| `deterministic` | inputs, rules, command, transition, or validation can be expressed reliably in code | coordinator or service |\n| `model` | the phase requires semantic interpretation, synthesis, ranking, investigation, or another bounded probabilistic judgement | focused agent or model call |\n\nPrefer deterministic phases for known commands, parsing, schema validation,\nbranch/state transitions, diff capture, policy checks, test execution, hashing,\ndeduplication, persistence, and other mechanical work. It remains conditional on four policy choices: what revisions may be reviewed, who may approve scope changes and risk acceptance, which verification commands are authoritative, and whether the workflow may create commits or only prepare a working-tree change.\n\n## 1. Outcome contract\n\nGoal: produce a remediated software revision whose identified material defects are resolved or explicitly dispositioned, and whose acceptance is supported by independent, revision-bound evidence.\n\nRequirements:\n\n- `R1` Review an immutable source snapshot against an immutable review contract.\n- `R2` Record findings as falsifiable, evidence-backed claims.\n- `R3` Permit remediation only within an approved write scope.\n- `R4` Independently verify the remediated revision; never accept the remediator’s self-report.\n- `R5` Reconcile every original finding as `fixed`, `not_reproduced`, `accepted_risk`, `superseded`, or `open`.\n- `R6` Run authoritative deterministic project gates on the exact candidate revision.\n- `R7` Preserve durable state sufficient to resume after any interruption.\n- `R8` Fail closed on stale evidence, unauthorized mutation, missing authority, or outcome-unknown effects.\n- `R9` Require accountable human decisions for contract changes, scope expansion, material risk acceptance, and consequential publication or deployment.\n\nTrigger:\n\n```text\nReviewRequest {\n  subject_ref,\n  base_revision,\n  candidate_revision,\n  review_contract_ref,\n  requested_by,\n  policy_version\n}\n```\n\nSuccessful terminal condition:\n\n```text\nACCEPTED only if:\n- all mandatory review dimensions were completed;\n- no unresolved blocking finding remains;\n- every accepted risk has a valid human decision receipt;\n- deterministic gates passed on final_revision;\n- independent verification inspected final_revision;\n- the actual change set remained within authorized scope;\n- all evidence and approvals are current and revision-bound.\n```\n\nOther terminal states:\n\n- `REJECTED`: authoritative human or policy rejection.\n- `FAILED`: bounded recovery exhausted or unrecoverable invariant violation.\n- `CANCELLED`: cancellation acknowledged before further effects.\n- `SUPERSEDED`: source, contract, or requested outcome was replaced.\n- `PARTIAL`: useful evidence exists, but acceptance was not established.\n\nNon-goals:\n\n- Selecting an orchestration framework.\n- Merging, deploying, or publishing without a separately authorized effect stage.\n- Allowing agents to redefine the review contract or accept risk.\n- Treating “review completed,” valid JSON, or green local tests as workflow success.\n\nCore invariants:\n\n- All findings, reviews, tests, and approvals name the exact revision they cover.\n- Reviewers cannot mutate the reviewed subject.\n- Remediators cannot modify workflow policy, gates, approvals, or evidence records.\n- A producer cannot be the sole verifier of its own output.\n- The coordinator alone advances authoritative workflow state.\n- Stale or unverified evidence never advances acceptance.\n\n## 2. Evidence ledger\n\nObserved:\n\n- `E1`: Repository guidance requires revision-sensitive artifacts and exact revision binding.\n- `E2`: Repository guidance distinguishes evidence, technical severity, policy disposition, and human verdict.\n- `E3`: `.agent-artifacts/<branch>/<workflow>/<revision>/` is the preferred artifact location, but only when safely ignored and untracked.\n- `E4`: The repository already conceptualizes review as read-only and remediation as a separately bounded implementation responsibility.\n\nInferred:\n\n- `I1`: The requested workflow primarily targets source-code review and remediation. This is falsified if the review subject is instead infrastructure, policy, documents, or external records.\n- `I2`: Multiple remediation iterations may be necessary, but concurrent writers are not necessary for the baseline design.\n\nAssumed:\n\n- `A1`: Git revisions or an equivalent immutable snapshot identity are available. Revalidate during intake.\n- `A2`: The project can declare deterministic verification commands. Revalidate before remediation begins.\n- `A3`: Reviewer and remediator can operate with separately enforced permissions. ## Workflow status: Conditional

The workflow is design-ready and runtime-neutral. It remains conditional on four policy choices: what revisions may be reviewed, who may approve scope changes and risk acceptance, which verification commands are authoritative, and whether the workflow may create commits or only prepare a working-tree change.

## 1. Outcome contract

Goal: produce a remediated software revision whose identified material defects are resolved or explicitly dispositioned, and whose acceptance is supported by independent, revision-bound evidence.

Requirements:

- `R1` Review an immutable source snapshot against an immutable review contract.
- `R2` Record findings as falsifiable, evidence-backed claims.
- `R3` Permit remediation only within an approved write scope.
- `R4` Independently verify the remediated revision; never accept the remediator’s self-report.
- `R5` Reconcile every original finding as `fixed`, `not_reproduced`, `accepted_risk`, `superseded`, or `open`.
- `R6` Run authoritative deterministic project gates on the exact candidate revision.
- `R7` Preserve durable state sufficient to resume after any interruption.
- `R8` Fail closed on stale evidence, unauthorized mutation, missing authority, or outcome-unknown effects.
- `R9` Require accountable human decisions for contract changes, scope expansion, material risk acceptance, and consequential publication or deployment.

Trigger:

```text
ReviewRequest {
  subject_ref,
  base_revision,
  candidate_revision,
  review_contract_ref,
  requested_by,
  policy_version
}
```

Successful terminal condition:

```text
ACCEPTED only if:
- all mandatory review dimensions were completed;
- no unresolved blocking finding remains;
- every accepted risk has a valid human decision receipt;
- deterministic gates passed on final_revision;
- independent verification inspected final_revision;
- the actual change set remained within authorized scope;
- all evidence and approvals are current and revision-bound.
```

Other terminal states:

- `REJECTED`: authoritative human or policy rejection.
- `FAILED`: bounded recovery exhausted or unrecoverable invariant violation.
- `CANCELLED`: cancellation acknowledged before further effects.
- `SUPERSEDED`: source, contract, or requested outcome was replaced.
- `PARTIAL`: useful evidence exists, but acceptance was not established.

Non-goals:

- Selecting an orchestration framework.
- Merging, deploying, or publishing without a separately authorized effect stage.
- Allowing agents to redefine the review contract or accept risk.
- Treating “review completed,” valid JSON, or green local tests as workflow success.

Core invariants:

- All findings, reviews, tests, and approvals name the exact revision they cover.
- Reviewers cannot mutate the reviewed subject.
- Remediators cannot modify workflow policy, gates, approvals, or evidence records.
- A producer cannot be the sole verifier of its own output.
- The coordinator alone advances authoritative workflow state.
- Stale or unverified evidence never advances acceptance.

Record the artefact, its claimed scope, and a freshness signal such as a revision, date, generated marker, or governing source when available. Revalidate claims that materially affect scope, design, compatibility, safety, or verification. A durable artefact that conflicts with a current authoritative source becomes evidence of drift or an unresolved decision; it is not permission to ignore the conflict.\n\nRecord the evidence that changes the plan. Avoid architecture-first planning and speculative generality.\n\n### 4. Retire material uncertainty\n\nRank unknowns by impact, lateness cost, and reversibility. First inspect evidence that is safely available. Ask a targeted question only when the answer could materially change the outcome, scope, architecture, safety, compatibility, acceptance criteria, or an expensive-to-reverse decision.\n\nOtherwise proceed with an explicit assumption and a revalidation point. For a blocking unknown, produce a bounded investigation step containing:\n\n1. the decision or question;\n2. the cheapest safe investigation;\n3. required evidence and decision rule;\n4. scope or attempt bound;\n5. resulting branch in the plan.\n\nDo not disguise “investigate” as an implementation step. If evidence cannot yet support an implementation sequence, return an investigation plan and mark the implementation plan Blocked.\n\nBefore finalizing a material requirement or design decision, run a challenge pass: clarify ambiguous terms, expose assumptions, seek counterexamples, test consequences and credible alternatives, and state what evidence would change the conclusion. Select the design and transition path\n\nFor each consequential decision, compare credible alternatives against current constraints, complexity, coupling, compatibility, security, operability, testability, migration cost, and reversibility. Do not force alternatives for a routine local change.\n\nDo not silently reopen a rejected or deferred alternative. Require materially new evidence, a changed constraint or outcome, a falsified assumption, an elapsed review condition, or an explicit accountable-human request. Record:\n\n- **Owner**: the accountable role or person when known;\n- **Decision**: the exact choice or acceptance required;\n- **Evidence**: the observations, alternatives, risks, or experiment result the owner should review;\n- **Blocks**: the slices, contracts, or transition states that must not proceed before the decision;\n- **State**: `open`, `approved`, `rejected`, or `superseded` only when supported by evidence.\n\nUse gates selectively. Do not require approval between requirements, design, and tasks when no real human-owned decision exists, and never infer approval from silence or implementation progress.\n\nDescribe the chosen responsibilities, knowledge ownership, interfaces, data and control flow, invariants, side effects, failures, concurrency, and compatibility only to the depth relevant to the task. Prefer:\n\n- simple boundaries that hide volatile knowledge;\n- one authoritative owner for each rule or state;\n- small end-to-end slices over horizontal layers;\n- preparatory refactoring separated from behavioural change;\n- additive or reversible transition states before destructive cleanup;\n- explicit integration and removal of temporary compatibility code.\n\nFor Standard or Critical plans, create a compact **responsibility and interface map** before sequencing slices when multiple components, files, services, schemas, or modules must coordinate. - Case: `AWD-E1`

- Final response:

## Plan status: Conditional

The workflow design is runtime-neutral and ready to prototype. It remains conditional on three human-owned policy decisions: what constitutes an approval-required risk, who may accept residual risk, and the retention policy for prompts, evidence, and receipts.

Repository constraints used as governing evidence:

- `E1`: Evidence, explanation, automated checks, and policy thresholds are not approval or human judgment. [README.md](/home/mark/.local/state/codex-desktop/tmp/agent-skills-eval-96t1q4u2/repo/README.md)
- `E2`: Review artifacts and verdicts bind to an exact revision.
- `E3`: Automation may enforce a recorded verdict but may not invent one.
- `E4`: Repository-local workflow artifacts belong under `.agent-artifacts/<branch>/<workflow>/<revision>/`, provided that location is safely ignored.

## 1. Outcome contract

The workflow accepts one immutable review target and produces either:

1. an independently verified, policy-compliant remediation result;
2. a human decision packet for unresolved risk or authority;
3. a durable blocked/cancelled/failure result that can be resumed or diagnosed without reconstructing hidden agent memory.

Requirements:

- `R1` — Deterministic orchestration owns state transitions; agents submit typed proposals and claims.
- `R2` — Reviewer, remediator, and verifier have distinct authority.
- `R3` — Every material artifact binds to the exact target revision and accepted contract.
- `R4` — Retries are bounded, classified, and idempotent.
- `R5` — Every externally visible transition is durably checkpointed and resumable.
- `R6` — No remediation is accepted from self-reported completion alone.
- `R7` — Approval, residual-risk acceptance, scope expansion, and contract changes remain human-owned.
- `R8` — Process death, stale work, duplicate delivery, ambiguous external effects, and verification regressions have explicit recovery paths.

Non-goals:

- Selecting an orchestration framework, queue, database, model vendor, or deployment topology.
- Letting agents approve, merge, deploy, revise requirements, or accept risk.
- Treating repeated model sampling as independent verification.
- Designing repository-specific review criteria before inspecting the target repository.

Core invariants:

- `I1`: One authoritative workflow record exists for each run.
- `I2`: Accepted evidence always names its target revision, contract version, producer identity, and provenance.
- `I3`: A changed revision invalidates all prior revision-sensitive review and verification results.
- `I4`: No actor reviews or verifies its own material output.
- `I5`: An effect is never repeated merely because its acknowledgement was lost.
- `I6`: Resumption rebuilds context from durable state; conversation history is never authoritative.
- `I7`: Terminal status does not imply approval unless a valid human verdict receipt exists.

## 2. Authority model

| Actor | May do | Must not do |
|---|---|---|
| Coordinator | Validate handoffs, apply transition rules, issue leases, enforce budgets, persist receipts | Interpret evidence as human approval; author remediation |
| Reviewer | Inspect the bound target; report falsifiable findings and coverage limits | Modify the target; accept risk; approve or merge |
| Triage/policy component | Deterministically classify findings using approved policy | Lower severity through model judgment; dismiss findings without evidence |
| Remediator | Modify only the accepted scope; run permitted checks; return evidence | Change the accepted contract; suppress findings; approve its own work |
| Independent verifier | Reproduce findings, inspect the remediation, run independent checks, report residual risk | Repair the work being verified; accept residual risk |
| Human owner | Approve scope or contract changes, waive/accept risk, resolve policy questions, cancel | Delegate accountability implicitly through silence |
| Effect executor | Perform separately authorized external effects and return receipts | Decide whether the effect is appropriate |
| Recovery operator | Break stale leases, reconcile ambiguous effects, resume or terminate runs | Alter historical receipts or fabricate completion evidence |

Separation must be based on execution identity and context isolation, not merely different prompts. At minimum, the verifier receives the original contract, review findings, resulting diff, and verification criteria—but not the remediator’s persuasive narrative as an authority source.

## 3. Authoritative state machine

```text
NEW
  → TARGET_BOUND
  → REVIEWING
  → REVIEW_READY
      ├─ no actionable findings → VERIFYING
      ├─ actionable findings    → REMEDIATION_PLANNED
      ├─ human decision needed  → AWAITING_DECISION
      └─ invalid target         → BLOCKED

REMEDIATION_PLANNED
  → REMEDIATING
  → REMEDIATION_READY
  → VERIFYING
      ├─ accepted                       → READY_FOR_HUMAN_VERDICT
      ├─ correctable findings remain    → REMEDIATION_PLANNED
      ├─ contract/scope conflict        → AWAITING_DECISION
      ├─ target became stale            → SUPERSEDED
      └─ retry/recovery exhausted       → BLOCKED

READY_FOR_HUMAN_VERDICT
  ├─ approved       → COMPLETED
  ├─ changes wanted → REMEDIATION_PLANNED
  ├─ rejected       → REJECTED
  └─ target changed → SUPERSEDED
```

Cross-cutting states:

- `PAUSED`: deliberately quiescent with no active lease.
- `RECOVERING`: reconciling a worker loss or uncertain effect.
- `CANCELLING`: cancellation requested; active work is being stopped.
- `CANCELLED`: terminal cancellation with retained evidence.
- `EXPIRED`: a wait, approval, or target-binding validity window elapsed.
- `BLOCKED`: cannot safely progress without new evidence, authority, or capability.
- `SUPERSEDED`: another target revision or decision replaced this run.
- `FAILED`: internal invariant or unrecoverable system failure—not an ordinary review rejection.

Every transition requires:

```text
expected_state + expected_workflow_version
actor_identity + actor_authority
command_id
validated input artifact references
transition result
durable event/receipt
```

Use compare-and-swap or equivalent optimistic concurrency. A worker never writes the next workflow state directly; it submits a handoff that the coordinator validates and applies.

## 4. Durable record model

```typescript
type WorkflowRecord = {
  workflowId: WorkflowId
  version: number
  state: WorkflowState
  target: TargetBinding
  contract: ContractSnapshot
  policyVersion: string
  instructionSetVersion: string
  activeLease?: Lease
  iteration: number
  budgets: BudgetState
  artifactRefs: ArtifactRef[]
  findingLedger: FindingRecord[]
  decisionRefs: DecisionReceipt[]
  effectRefs: EffectReceipt[]
  lastTransition: TransitionReceipt
  createdAt: Timestamp
  updatedAt: Timestamp
}
```

`TargetBinding` contains repository identity, base revision, exact reviewed revision, working-tree digest if applicable, and relevant dependency/configuration fingerprints.

Store large prompts, logs, diffs, and tool output as immutable artifacts referenced by digest. Keep only compact, redacted summaries in model context.

## 5. Typed handoffs

All handoffs share an envelope:

```typescript
type Handoff<TKind, TPayload> = {
  schemaVersion: string
  handoffId: UUID
  workflowId: WorkflowId
  kind: TKind
  producer: {
    role: Role
    executionId: string
    modelOrToolVersion?: string
  }
  target: TargetBinding
  contractVersion: string
  workflowVersionRead: number
  attempt: number
  createdAt: Timestamp
  payload: TPayload
  evidence: EvidenceRef[]
  uncertainty: Uncertainty[]
  contentDigest: Digest
}
```

Principal payloads:

```typescript
type ReviewReport = {
  coverage: ReviewCoverage
  findings: Finding[]
  checksRun: CheckResult[]
  limitations: Limitation[]
  recommendation: "verify_clean" | "remediate" | "human_decision" | "blocked"
}

  ruleOrRequirementRefs: string[]
  location: RevisionBoundLocation[]
  claim: string
  severity: Severity
  consequence: string
  reproduction?: Reproduction
  falsificationAttempts: EvidenceRef[]
  confidenceBasis: string
  remediationConstraint?: string
}

type RemediationTask = {
  taskId: StableId
  acceptedFindingIds: StableId[]
  allowedScope: ResourceScope
  forbiddenEffects: Capability[]
  requiredChecks: CheckSpecification[]
  completionContract: CompletionCriterion[]
}

type RemediationResult = {
  taskId: StableId
  resultRevision: RevisionId
  changeDigest: Digest
  findingDisposition: FindingDisposition[]

or\n  described with their actual limits.\n\n--ADAPTIVE--\n# Adaptive planning contract\n\nUse this reference when a model generates the workflow topology for the current\nrun rather than executing a record receipt\n```\n\n## Planner boundary\n\nThe planner may decide:\n\n- decomposition;\n- sequencing and dependencies;\n- safe read-only fan-out;\n- candidate worker roles from registered IDs;\n- bounded loops/repeated checks;\n- aggregation shape;\n- estimated worker/token/cost budget;\n- proposed mutation scopes from allowed roots.\n\nThe planner may **not**:\n\n- create or install tools/ACP agents;\n- invent an executable command or arbitrary code primitive;\n- widen filesystem, network, credential or environment scope;\n- change permission policy;\n- approve its own plan;\n- bypass workflow limits;\n- mutate the target repository while planning;\n- silently replace a rejected/invalid graph with a simpler one.\n\nTreat planner output as untrusted data.\n\n## Structured envelope\n\nRequire structured output rather than prose another agent must reinterpret. The\nexact schema can vary, but should preserve:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"objective\": \"...\",\n  \"assumptions\": [],\n  \"steps\": [],\n  \"stopConditions\": [],\n  \"maxRetries\": 0,\n  \"estimatedAgents\": 0,\n  \"estimatedTokenBudget\": 0,\n  \"graph\": []\n}\n```\n\nEach planned worker step should identify enough policy-relevant information to\nvalidate it mechanically, for example:\n\n- stable step ID;\n- kind/type;\n- registered primitive ID;\n- dependencies;\n- read-only vs mutating status;\n- permitted scope;\n- optional concurrency group;\n- task/prompt intent;\n- expected structured result when control flow depends on it.\n\nDo not require fields that the runtime/policy cannot use. The purpose is to make\nmaterial planning decisions inspectable and enforceable.\n\n## Deterministic validation\n\nValidate the envelope and executable graph separately.\n\nAt minimum check:\n\n- JSON/schema validity;\n- known graph entry types for the installed Mastra version;\n- registered/allowed primitive IDs;\n- stable unique step IDs;\n- valid dependency references and no accidental cycles;\n- valid mappings and schema flow;\n- allowed filesystem/resource roots;\n- maximum agents/tasks and concurrency;\n- maximum retry/round counts;\n- token/cost ceilings where the environment exposes them;\n- bounded loops and explicit stop/no-progress conditions;\n- mutation scopes and concurrent-write safety;\n- no executable code/command injection through planner-controlled fields.\n\nA syntactically valid graph is not automatically policy-valid.\n\n## Mutation and concurrency\n\nPrefer adaptive fan-out for independent analysis, search, review, classification,\nor other read-mostly work.\n\nFor repository mutation, default to one sequential mutation lane. A planner may\npropose parallel writers only when deterministic validation can establish\ndisjoint mutable scopes or the runtime provides isolated workspaces plus an\nexplicit integration phase.\n\nIf safe independence cannot be established, rewrite/reject the concurrency plan;\ndo not rely on the planner's assertion that edits will not conflict.\n\n## Approval boundary\n\nRequire preview/approval before execution when the accepted plan introduces\nmaterial mutation, external effects, elevated permissions, unfamiliar resource\nscope, or material cost/parallelism.\n\nApproval should cover the things that actually determine blast radius:\n\n- objective and material assumptions;\n- exact graph identity/digest;\n- registered workers/tools;\n- mutation/resource scope;\n- permissions/effects;\n- concurrency;\n- agent/task/retry/token/cost budget;\n- stop conditions.\n\nApproval of only the original natural-language request is not approval of an\narbitrarily generated execution graph.\n\nA read-only, low-cost plan may auto-run only when existing policy or explicit user\nauthorization permits it.\n\n## Persistence and replan semantics\n\nPersist the exact approved graph and a stable identity/digest with the run.\n\nResume means continue/replay the **same approved graph** under the runtime's actual\nresume semantics. Replanning is a new proposal with a new graph identity that\nmust pass validation and any required approval again.\n\nDo not overwrite the prior graph and call the result a resume.\n\nIf source state, branch revision, permissions, policy, registered primitives, or\nother material preconditions changed, revalidate before continuing and invalidate\nprior evidence where necessary.\n\n## Repair policy\n\nIf planner output is malformed or fails a correctable structural constraint, one\nbounded repair attempt may be appropriate. Return the concrete validation errors\nand require a complete replacement proposal.\n\nDo not repair around:\n\n- missing authority;\n- forbidden scope;\n- unavailable required capability;\n- unsafe parallel mutation that cannot be isolated;\n- a budget the task inherently exceeds without human acceptance;\n- stale source assumptions that require fresh investigation.\n\nThose conditions require a blocked/replanned decision, not prompt persistence.\n\n## Run receipt\n\nRecord enough to inspect and reproduce what happened:\n\n- task/objective;\n- plan/graph identity and digest;\n- material assumptions;\n- validation result and policy version/settings;\n- approval decision when applicable;\n- actual started/completed/failed steps;\n- worker/runtime versions where available;\n- token/cost/concurrency observations where available;\n- repository/source revision before and after;\n- deterministic verification evidence;\n- termination reason;\n- whether the run is resumable, requires replan, or is terminal.\n\nDo not fabricate lifecycle guarantees the installed Mastra version does not\nprovide.\n\n--RUNTIME--\n# Mastra dynamic-workflow runtime\n\nUse this reference when implementing, changing, validating, storing, or running a\nMastra dynamic workflow.\n\n## Runtime role\n\nMastra is the orchestration runtime. A dynamic workflow is persisted as a\nJSON-compatible graph that references registered agents, tools, workflows, and\ncontrol-flow primitives by stable IDs.\n\nKeep these responsibilities separate:\n\n- **Mastra**: graph execution, ordering, mappings, control flow, state, storage,\n  validation, run lifecycle and registered primitive resolution.\n- **Application/Mastra integration and policy layer**: approvals, authority,\n  allowed primitive IDs, filesystem/network/resource scope, effect boundaries,\n  and concurrency/cost limits supplied to or enforced around the runtime.\n- **Adaptive planner, when used**: propose task decomposition and a graph only.\n- **ACP worker**: repository reasoning, file changes, commands/tests, and other\n  coding-agent capabilities permitted by its environment.\n- **Filesystem / explicit state**: shared truth between separate worker calls.\n\nMastra executes workflow policy supplied by the application/integration layer; do\nnot attribute deployment-specific approval or authority policy to Mastra itself.\nDo not insert a model-backed supervisor merely to coordinate a known graph.\n\n## Version preflight\n\nBefore writing code:\n\n1. inspect installed `@mastra/core`, `@mastra/acp`, and storage versions;\n2. inspect the installed dynamic-workflow docs/types/source for the exact graph\n   schema and APIs;\n3. compare current remote docs only when useful;\n4. upgrade related packages deliberately rather than mixing incompatible eras.\n\nDynamic workflows require `@mastra/core >= 1.58.0`. ACP support requires\n`@mastra/core >= 1.34.0`. Treat these as minimum feature versions, not recommended\nhard pins.\n\nFor a new local project the minimum shape commonly includes:\n\n```bash\nnpm install @mastra/core @mastra/acp @mastra/libsql\n```\n\nAlso install or make available the selected ACP executable/adapter if coding\nworkers are required.\n\n## Storage and registry\n\nDynamic workflows are stored definitions, so configure Mastra storage. For a\nlocal-only project, LibSQL is a reasonable default unless the user already has a\nstorage adapter or requests another one:\n\n```ts\nimport { Mastra } from \"@mastra/core/mastra\";\nimport { LibSQLStore } from \"@mastra/libsql\";\n\nexport const mastra = new Mastra({\n  storage: new LibSQLStore({\n    id: \"mastra-storage\",\n    url: \"file:./mastra.db\",\n  }),\n  tools: {\n    // registered tools referenced by dynamic workflow toolId\n  },\n  agents: {\n    // ordinary registered Mastra agents referenced by dynamic workflow agentId\n  },\n});\n```\n\nUse stable primitive IDs. A generated graph may reference only IDs already\nregistered and allowed by the application's policy layer.\n\n## ACP workers in a dynamic workflow\n\n`@mastra/acp` exposes two relevant integration forms:\n\n- `AcpAgent`: wraps an ACP process as a Mastra subagent with agent-style methods;\n- `createACPTool()`: wraps an ACP process as a Mastra tool that accepts a task and\n  returns output.\n\nFor a dynamic workflow that needs a direct coding worker **without a model\nsupervisor**, `createACPTool()` is the simplest stable conceptual boundary: the\nworkflow references a registered tool and the tool launches the ACP agent.\n\nExample shape:\n\n```ts\nimport { createACPTool } from \"@mastra/acp\";\n\nexport const coderTool = createACPTool({\n  id: \"coder\",\n  description: \"ACP coding worker for repository tasks.\",\n  command: process.execPath,\n  args: [\"/absolute/path/to/the/acp-adapter.js\"],\n  cwd: repo,\n});\n```\n\nThen register `coderTool` under `tools` and reference its registered ID from a\n`tool` graph entry.\n\nIf the project deliberately uses a real Mastra supervisor `Agent`, an `AcpAgent`\nmay instead be attached as that agent's subagent. Do not add such a supervisor\nsolely to make the dynamic workflow work.\n\n**Important:** exact registration support has changed across Mastra versions. A\nhistorical tested combination had a failure when a bare `AcpAgent` was registered\ndirectly in `new Mastra({ agents: ... })`. Check the installed current source\nbefore relying on either that failure or a workaround. See\n`references/troubleshooting.md` from the main skill when the issue actually\nappears.\n\n## Dynamic definition\n\nA stored workflow definition includes, at minimum, an ID, input/output schema and\nan executable graph. Optional state/request-context/metadata fields depend on the\ncurrent definition contract.\n\nUse JSON Schema inside stored definitions. Verify the current supported graph\nentry types from installed docs/source before authoring a non-trivial graph. The\nset has included agent, tool, mapping, nested workflow, parallel, conditional,\nforeach, loop and timing entries, but this reference is deliberately not the\nsource of truth for the installed version.\n\n### Data-flow rules\n\n- Give every call site a stable descriptive `id`.\n- Map workflow input and prior results explicitly.\n- Match mapping keys to the primitive actually invoked.\n- Use structured output when branch/loop logic depends on semantic worker output.\n- Keep control-flow inputs machine-evaluable rather than asking a later model to\n  reinterpret prose.\n- Keep mappings within the shapes the installed stored-workflow DSL supports.\n- Treat repository state as authoritative for sequential code edits; prompt text\n  is not a substitute for observing the actual working tree.\n\nA `createACPTool()` worker and an agent-style primitive may expose different input\nand output envelopes. Inspect the installed types/reference and build mappings to\nthat actual shape rather than assuming `prompt/text` or `task/output` from an\nolder release.\n\n## Validation\n\nBefore upsert/registration:\n\n- validate JSON/schema structure;\n- verify every referenced primitive ID exists and is permitted;\n- verify mapping expressions and upstream/downstream schemas;\n- reject unsupported graph types;\n- reject unbounded loops/retries;\n- enforce maximum fan-out/concurrency and cost/task budgets;\n- reject unsafe overlapping mutations;\n- ensure adaptive planner output cannot introduce code, commands, tools,\n  permissions, roots or credentials through graph data.\n\nAllow one bounded repair of malformed planner output only when the repair can be\nvalidated deterministically. Never silently execute a different simplified graph.\n\n## Persistence and execution\n\nMastra can persist dynamic workflow definitions and expose them through stored\nworkflow APIs/client operations. Use the project's existing route/client style.\nCurrent Mastra documentation has exposed stored workflow management under\n`/api/stored/workflows`, but that path is **version-sensitive guidance, not a\nstable contract**. Before using or generating code for it, verify the exact route\nand operation shape against the installed Mastra version's docs/types/source or,\nwhen no version is installed yet, the current official documentation. Follow the\nsource-precedence and verification record in `references/remote-docs.md` rather\nthan hard-coding this path from the skill text alone.\n\nFor adaptive runs, persist the exact approved definition with an immutable\nidentity or digest and the policy settings that validated it. Replanning produces\na new graph identity and a new validation/approval decision.\n\nDo not claim cross-process/session resumability merely because a workflow can be\nstored. Verify the installed run lifecycle, suspension/resume semantics and\npersistence guarantees for the actual runtime version.\n\n## Completion test\n\nStatic file generation is not sufficient evidence of success. When the environment\nallows it:\n\n1. instantiate/configure Mastra;\n2. validate or register/upsert the definition;\n3. load the stored workflow;\n4. invoke the narrowest representative input;\n5. inspect real workflow/worker output and repository state;\n6. run the relevant deterministic checker or acceptance check.\n\nIf live ACP authentication or network access prevents step 4+, validate Mastra's\nconfiguration/definition separately and report the exact remaining blocker.\n--REMOTE--\n# Current documentation and source precedence\n\nUse this reference before writing version-sensitive Mastra dynamic-workflow or\nACP integration code.\n\nThese APIs are changing quickly. Treat remembered API shapes and this skill's\nhistorical examples as lower authority than the user's installed version and\ncurrent canonical documentation.\n\n## Source precedence\n\nWhen a Mastra project already exists:\n\n1. **Installed package docs, types, and source** for the exact project version.\n2. **Current official Mastra documentation** when installed material is missing\n   or conceptual guidance is needed.\n3. **Current ACP documentation/registry** for worker compatibility and\n   distribution metadata.\n4. **This skill's references** for stable design rules and previously observed\n   implementation pitfalls.\n\nWhen no project/packages exist, start with current official Mastra documentation,\nthen choose versions together rather than mixing old core and new integration\npackages casually.\n\nA current remote page can be ahead of an installed package. Never use a newer\nremote example to override the types/source of the version the project actually\nruns without deliberately upgrading it.\n\n## Mastra documentation discovery\n\nStart with Mastra's agent-friendly documentation index:\n\n`https://mastra.ai/llms.txt`\n\nRelevant current areas include:\n\n- dynamic workflows: `https://mastra.ai/docs/workflows/dynamic-workflows.md`\n- ACP: `https://mastra.ai/docs/agents/acp.md`\n- `AcpAgent`: `https://mastra.ai/reference/acp/acp-agent.md`\n- `createACPTool()`: `https://mastra.ai/reference/acp/create-acp-tool.md`\n\nPrefer the Markdown form when available. Verify graph entry types, mapping syntax, schemas, persistence and run\nlifecycle against the installed/current release rather than reconstructing them\nfrom memory.\n\n## ACP discovery\n\nACP documentation index:\n\n`https://agentclientprotocol.com/llms.txt`\n\nRegistry:\n\n`https://agentclientprotocol.com/get-started/registry`\n\nMachine-readable current registry:\n\n`https://cdn.agentclientprotocol.com/registry/v1/latest/registry.json`\n\nUse the registry when resolving an unfamiliar worker or checking whether a named\ncoding harness currently exposes an ACP distribution. Do not copy the registry's\nfull agent list into active instructions.\n\n## Claude Code Workflows as a semantic reference\n\nClaude Code's implementation is a useful reference for the *workflow model*, not\na Mastra API contract:\n\n- documentation index: `https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt`\n- dynamic workflows: `https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows`\n\nTransfer durable semantics such as:\n\n- orchestration held by executable runtime state rather than a lead model's\n  context;\n- intermediate results retained by the workflow rather than replayed into a\n  supervisor conversation;\n- explicit fan-out/fan-in and bounded loops;\n- generated orchestration inspectable before execution;\n- progress, cancellation and resumability as runtime concerns;\n- coding workers performing filesystem/shell work while orchestration code\n  coordinates them.\n\nDo **not** copy Claude-specific JavaScript APIs, agent caps, permission behaviour,\nfilesystem paths, or session-resume semantics into a Mastra implementation unless\nthe user explicitly asks for Claude Code itself.\n\n## Verification record\n\nWhen a version-sensitive decision materially affects the implementation, record\nat least:\n\n- installed package/version or current remote source;\n- the relevant API/type/source location;\n- the date checked;\n- any gap between current remote docs and the installed version;\n- whether a workaround is current behaviour or only a historical observation.\n\nThis keeps temporary compatibility knowledge from becoming permanent skill law.\n\n--README--\n# Agent Skills\n\nA catalogue of reusable **Agent Skills** and orchestrating agent definitions for\nsoftware engineering, learning, workflow improvement, and accountable\nAI-assisted delivery.\n\nSkills are portable procedure packages. Agents coordinate skills, lifecycle,\nstate, delegation, and human responsibility boundaries.\n\n## Repository structure\n\n```text\nagents/\n  <agent-name>.md          # orchestration and workflow state\n\n<skill-name>/\n  SKILL.md                 # canonical Agent Skills entry point\n  references/              # optional, loaded on demand\n  scripts/                 # optional deterministic helpers\n  assets/                  # optional output resources\n```\n\n## Packaging rules\n\nEvery skill is self-contained and can be installed by copying its own directory.\n\n- The entry point is `<skill-name>/SKILL.md`.\n- Supporting files live inside that skill's directory.\n- A skill must not depend on a repository-level shared folder, parent path,\n  another skill's directory, or an agent definition.\n- Small process guidance may be duplicated when that preserves portability.\n- Relative references should be direct from `SKILL.md`; avoid nested reference\n  chains.\n- Keep active `SKILL.md` instructions under 500 lines. Move optional detail into\n  focused references.\n\nCanonical frontmatter uses only specification fields:\n\n```yaml\n---\nname: skill-name\ndescription: What the skill does and when to use it.\nlicense: Apache-2.0                # optional\ncompatibility: Requires git ...   # optional\nmetadata:                         # optional string mapping\n  example.key: \"value\"\nallowed-tools: Bash(git:*) Read   # optional, experimental\n---\n```\n\nRuntime-specific properties must not be added as new top-level fields to the\ncanonical skill. Store portable extension information under namespaced\n`metadata`, then translate it into a generated harness adapter when needed.\n\n## Agent workflow artefacts\n\nRepository-local supporting artefacts created by agents or skills use one\ncanonical root:\n\n```text\n.agent-artifacts/<work-branch>/<workflow>/<artifact>\n```\n\nUse the exact short work-branch name and preserve `/` as path separators. For\nexample, artefacts for `feature/PAY-1234` live under\n`.agent-artifacts/feature/PAY-1234/`. A PR-scoped workflow uses the PR head\nbranch; a working-tree workflow uses the active branch. When no named branch can\nbe resolved for a revision-bound operation, use\n`.agent-artifacts/detached/<full-head-sha>/...`.\n\nRevision-sensitive workflows should add a revision directory beneath the\nworkflow when one is available, for example:\n\n```text\n.agent-artifacts/feature/PAY-1234/review/<head-sha>/report.md\n.agent-artifacts/feature/PAY-1234/review/<head-sha>/risk-map.json\n.agent-artifacts/feature/PAY-1234/implement/<commit-sha>/implementation-evidence.json\n.agent-artifacts/feature/PAY-1234/create-pr/<head-sha>/body.md\n```\n\nFor an uncommitted working-tree review, use a clearly non-revision label such as\n`review/working-tree/` and bind the artefact content to the reviewed base plus\nworking-tree evidence or digest.\n\nThis root is intentionally suitable for a single `.gitignore` entry. Before\nwriting repository-local supporting artefacts, verify the root is ignored and\ncontains no tracked files. Never add or modify ignore rules implicitly. If the\ncanonical root is not safely ignored, return the artefact inline or keep it in\norchestration state when possible; if an on-disk artefact is required to\ncontinue, stop with the missing storage prerequisite rather than writing to an\narbitrary repository path or external temporary directory.\n\nThe convention applies to workflow-supporting outputs such as review reports,\nrisk maps, implementation-evidence packets, resumable checkpoints, generated\nhandoffs, and temporary PR bodies. It does not relocate user-requested product\nor repository deliverables that are meant to be tracked as part of the change.\n\n## Public and internal skills\n\nPublic skills may be invoked directly. Workflow-internal modules sit behind an\nagent interface and fail closed without the owning agent's orchestration state.\n\nInternal modules use canonical metadata such as:\n\n```yaml\nmetadata:\n  mhingston.internal: \"true\"\n  mhingston.owner-agent: \"pr-review\"\n  mhingston.user-invocable: \"false\"\n```\n\nThis metadata communicates intent but is not an authorization boundary. The\nmodule's body must still require its owning agent's exact context and return\n`REQUIRED_ORCHESTRATOR_CONTEXT` when invoked directly. A runtime adapter may map\nthe metadata to its native visibility mechanism.\n\n## Agent catalogue\n\n| Agent | Use it for |\n| --- | --- |\n| [`implement`](agents/implement.md) | Orchestrate a ready ticket through a ticket-keyed feature branch, delegated behaviour-first implementation with falsifiable verification, independent technical review, explicit contract reconciliation, full build/test gates, and pull-request creation. |\n| [`pr-review`](agents/pr-review.md) | Require a current independent technical review and revision-bound risk map, provide proportionate comprehension support, redirect unresolved architecture decisions upstream, prepare explicit human judgement, and record the human verdict without approving or merging. |\n| [`refine`](agents/refine.md) | Classify selected work, clarify unresolved decisions, refine one bounded ticket or split larger clear work into agent-ready vertical slices, resolve publication targets, and update the selected tracker after human approval. |\n\n## Suggested workflows\n\nThe catalogue is composable rather than one mandatory SDLC. Start with the\nsmallest workflow that owns the outcome; add adjacent skills only when their\nextra evidence or control is useful. Square brackets below indicate optional\nstages rather than required ceremony.\n\n| Goal | Suggested flow | Notes |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Deliver a ticket | `refine` → [`plan`] → `implement` → [`pr-review`] | `plan` is useful when design or uncertainty deserves a separate non-mutating pass. `implement` already owns implementation, independent technical review, contract reconciliation, final project gates, and `create-pr`. Do not create a tester,\ncommitter, poller, or router agent merely to rediscover an invocation the system\nalready knows.\n\nFor every `model` phase define:\n\n- its single decision or responsibility;\n- the evidence and context it may inspect;\n- the structured result it must return;\n- the effects it may propose and the effects it may perform;\n- deterministic validation after the result;\n- write/resource boundaries;\n- retry and escalation behaviour;\n- the evidence required before the coordinator accepts its completion claim.\n\nPrefer one purpose per worker. Split agents when responsibilities require\ndifferent permissions, independent judgement, separate context, or different\nacceptance contracts—not to create ceremonial parallelism.\n\n## 3. Make deterministic orchestration authoritative\n\nRepresent the workflow as an explicit state machine or dependency graph. The\ncoordinator, not model conversation state, owns:\n\n- allowed states and transitions;\n- phase ordering and dependencies;\n- run/task/phase identities;\n- source versions and revision identities;\n- attempt and retry counts;\n- approvals and decision receipts;\n- effect receipts and reconciliation state;\n- terminal acceptance or failure;\n- cancellation, pause, expiry, stale, and superseded states.\n\nDefault transitions to **not accepted** until their evidence is established.\nReject invalid transitions rather than asking a model to reason around them.\n\nSeparate these concepts explicitly:\n\n1. **Phase execution status** — did the phase execute its assigned function?\n2. **Phase result validity** — did its output parse and satisfy semantic checks?\n3. **Workflow acceptance** — does the current exact state satisfy the end-to-end\n   outcome and all required gates?\n\nA test runner can successfully execute a red test suite. A reviewer can\nsuccessfully complete a review that identifies blockers. An agent can return\nvalid JSON containing false claims. None of those imply workflow acceptance.\n\n## 4. Design handoffs as typed claims\n\nPrefer structured handoffs over free-form conversational continuation when later\nlogic depends on the result. Treat a model result as a **manifest of claims**, not\nas proof those claims are true.\n\nFor each handoff define:\n\n- schema/version and required fields;\n- stable identifiers for source state and relevant revision;\n- status vocabulary with unambiguous semantics;\n- artifact references rather than embedding bulky context where practical;\n- provenance required by the next phase;\n- semantic invariants beyond syntax;\n- fields the model is not authorised to determine.\n\nUse the smallest output schema that lets the next deterministic control or worker\nact without reinterpreting prose. Avoid one generic envelope when distinct result\ntypes have materially different semantics.\n\nKeep bulky evidence outside the model response when a durable artifact or store\nis more appropriate. The handoff should point to evidence, not duplicate an\nunbounded transcript.\n\n## 5. Gate claims independently\n\nFor every material claim ask what independent observation could prove it wrong.\nDesign gates that validate the world, not the agent's wording.\n\nExamples:\n\n| Claim | Stronger gate |\n| --- | --- |\n| \"I changed these files\" | compare the actual change set against the claimed paths and permitted scope |\n| \"tests pass\" | run the configured deterministic test command and record the exact result |\n| \"artifact written\" | verify path, existence, expected format, non-empty content, and state identity where relevant |\n| \"review found no blockers\" | require an independent review bound to the exact revision rather than the implementer's self-report |\n| \"external write completed\" | read back the authoritative external state or durable effect receipt |\n\nA gate should record **what it checked**, not only pass/fail. Preserve evidence\nfor successful checks as well as failures so a later operator can answer what was\nactually verified.\n\nDistinguish deterministic validation from semantic evaluation. Use human or model\nevaluation only for properties that executable checks cannot establish, and keep\nthe evaluator independent of the producer when independence matters.\n\n## 6. Separate capability from authority\n\nModel-visible tools describe what a worker *can attempt*; they do not necessarily\nbound what it can change. A shell, scripting runtime, generic filesystem tool,\nGit command, database client, or broad API can bypass a nominally narrow tool\nprofile.\n\nFor every mutating worker define independently enforced boundaries where the\nharness supports them:\n\n- allowed repository paths or write set;\n- protected control-plane paths;\n- allowed external resources, tenants, environments, and operations;\n- network destinations;\n- credential scope;\n- branch/workspace ownership;\n- maximum effect size or rate;\n- actions requiring separate approval.\n\nProtect the machinery that determines success: workflow code, policy, gate\nconfiguration, approval state, evidence stores, and evaluator configuration\nshould normally be outside the worker's write authority.\n\nWhen the runtime cannot enforce a write set before the fact, compare state before\nand after the worker and fail closed on unauthorized mutation. Include reversions\nand deletions in the change set: restoring a previously dirty path is still a\nmutation. Do not automatically discard pre-existing user changes merely to clean\nup an agent violation.\n\nFor parallel writers, require isolated mutable state plus an explicit integration\nowner. Tool separation without state isolation is not safe parallelism.\n\n## 7. Give different failures different retry semantics\n\nDo not use one generic retry loop. Classify failures and choose the smallest unit\nthat can correct them:\n\n- **Malformed structured result** — re-prompt the same model session with the\n  schema error when preserving context helps and the retry is bounded.\n- **Failed claim gate** — return the concrete violations to the same responsible\n  worker when correction is in scope and evidence has not gone stale.\n- **Deterministic transient failure** — retry in code only when the operation is\n  safe/idempotent and bounded by explicit error classes, timeout, and backoff.\n- **Failed implementation hypothesis** — diagnose from new evidence; do not layer\n  equivalent speculative fixes. Switch strategy or stop when attempts no longer\n  retire uncertainty.\n- **Independent verification** — use a fresh reviewer/evaluator context when the\n  purpose is to avoid producer anchoring.\n- **Missing authority, stale source, policy denial, incompatible state, or unsafe\n  scope expansion** — do not retry; block, replan, or request the accountable\n  decision.\n\nDefine attempt, token, time, cost, and transition budgets where material. Detect\nno-progress states such as repeated equivalent actions, unchanged failures,\noscillation, duplicate workers, or late results against superseded state.\n\n## 8. Design durable interruption and resumption\n\nIf work can outlive one model context or process, persist authoritative progress\noutside conversation memory. Define:\n\n- checkpoint identity and schema;\n- when a checkpoint is written;\n- exact source/repository/external state identity it describes;\n\nFILES\nREADME.md\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

Include the\npaths that break orchestration rather than only happy-path task completion:\n\n- invalid transition rejection;\n- malformed and semantically invalid model results;\n- unauthorized tool or write attempts;\n- worker modification of protected control-plane state;\n- stale source/revision results;\n- duplicate or late workers;\n- retry exhaustion and no-progress escalation;\n- termination before and after consequential effects;\n- restart and reconciliation;\n- approval expiry, rejection, amendment, and supersession;\n- cancellation and partial completion;\n- independent-review revision binding;\n- overall acceptance when phases succeed but outcome gates fail.\n\nUse deterministic tests for deterministic properties. Use model-based or human\nsemantic evaluation only where interpretation is genuinely required, and pin the\nevaluator inputs and versions when comparing runs.\n\n## Output contract\n\nReturn the smallest design package that preserves the following:\n\n1. **Workflow status** — `Ready`, `Conditional`, or `Blocked`, with the reason.\n2. **Outcome contract** — `R#` requirements, triggers, terminal states, invariants,\n   scope, non-goals, authoritative inputs, and completion evidence.\n3. **Evidence ledger** — compact `E#`, `I#`, `A#`, and `Q#` entries that materially\n   constrain the design.\n4. **Phase map** — ordered/state-machine view with `human`, `deterministic`, and\n   `model` kinds; owner, purpose, dependencies, inputs, outputs, effects, and why\n   each model phase requires model judgement.\n5. **State and authority model** — authoritative store, identities, transitions,\n   version/freshness rules, approval ownership, and pause/cancel/stale semantics.\n6. **Handoff contracts** — structured schemas, status semantics, artifact/provenance\n   references, and the claims each result makes.\n7. **Gate and acceptance map** — independent checks for material claims, phase\n   validity, exact-state binding, and final workflow acceptance.\n8. **Capability and mutation boundaries** — tools, enforced write/resource scope,\n   protected control plane, credentials, network, parallel-state ownership, and\n   approval-required effects.\n9. **Retry and recovery model** — failure classes, retry owner/unit, budgets,\n   no-progress detection, checkpoints, resume revalidation, reconciliation, and\n   uncertain-effect handling.\n10. **Observability and verification** — events/receipts required to reconstruct a\n    run plus deterministic trajectory and failure-path tests.\n11. **Human decisions and open questions** — unresolved authority or policy that\n    the workflow must not invent.\n\nInclude a Mermaid state or flow diagram when it materially improves comprehension,\nbut the textual contracts remain authoritative.\n\n## Stop and escalate\n\nReturn `Blocked` rather than inventing a workflow when:\n\n- the intended outcome or authority is materially unresolved;\n- a consequential effect has no safe permission or reconciliation model;\n- the workflow needs mutation but the available isolation or blast radius is\n  unacceptable;\n- a material model decision has no credible validation or accountable consumer;\n- external effects can become outcome-unknown with no idempotency/read-back path;\n- parallel workers share uncontrolled mutable state;\n- required acceptance evidence cannot be bound to the exact state it validates.\n\nReturn `Conditional` when bounded assumptions remain but their revalidation points\nand blocked transitions are explicit.\n\n## Quality gate\n\nBefore returning, verify that:\n\n- the workflow starts from an outcome, not an agent roster;\n- every model phase has a specific reason to require probabilistic judgement;\n- deterministic code owns expressible sequencing, validation, policy, and state;\n- model outputs are structured claims followed by independent checks where\n  correctness matters;\n- phase execution, result validity, and workflow acceptance are distinct;\n- capability lists are not mistaken for enforced write or effect authority;\n- the worker cannot silently rewrite the control plane that judges its work;\n- retries differ by failure semantics and are bounded;\n- durable state survives interruption and is revalidated on resume;\n- stale, duplicate, late, cancelled, and uncertain-effect paths are explicit;\n- independent verification is bound to the exact revision/state it inspected;\n- observability records evidence, not merely final verdicts;\n- trajectory tests cover policy, recovery, and failure paths as well as the happy\n  path;\n- consequential human decisions remain human-owned.\n\n## Evaluation\n\nWhen changing the description, applicability boundaries, or workflow behaviour,\nread [`references/evaluation-suite.md`](references/evaluation-suite.md) and run the\nmatched routing and outcome cases in a real harness when available. Keep sibling\nskills discoverable in both conditions and report routing as `not_verifiable`\nrather than substituting a classifier when the harness hides skill discovery.\nREADME\n# Agent Skills\n\nA catalogue of reusable **Agent Skills** and orchestrating agent definitions for\nsoftware engineering, learning, workflow improvement, and accountable\nAI-assisted delivery.\n\nSkills are portable procedure packages. Agents coordinate skills, lifecycle,\nstate, delegation, and human responsibility boundaries.\n\n## Repository structure\n\n```text\nagents/\n  <agent-name>.md          # orchestration and workflow state\n\n<skill-name>/\n  SKILL.md                 # canonical Agent Skills entry point\n  references/              # optional, loaded on demand\n  scripts/                 # optional deterministic helpers\n  assets/                  # optional output resources\n```\n\n## Packaging rules\n\nEvery skill is self-contained and can be installed by copying its own directory.\n\n- The entry point is `<skill-name>/SKILL.md`.\n- Supporting files live inside that skill's directory.\n- A skill must not depend on a repository-level shared folder, parent path,\n  another skill's directory, or an agent definition.\n- Small process guidance may be duplicated when that preserves portability.\n- Relative references should be direct from `SKILL.md`; avoid nested reference\n  chains.\n- Keep active `SKILL.md` instructions under 500 lines. Move optional detail into\n  focused references.\n\nCanonical frontmatter uses only specification fields:\n\n```yaml\n---\nname: skill-name\ndescription: What the skill does and when to use it.\nlicense: Apache-2.0                # optional\ncompatibility: Requires git ...   # optional\nmetadata:                         # optional string mapping\n  example.key: \"value\"\nallowed-tools: Bash(git:*) Read   # optional, experimental\n---\n```\n\nRuntime-specific properties must not be added as new top-level fields to the\ncanonical skill. Store portable extension information under namespaced\n`metadata`, then translate it into a generated harness adapter when needed.\n\n## Agent workflow artefacts\n\nRepository-local supporting artefacts created by agents or skills use one\ncanonical root:\n\n```text\n.agent-artifacts/<work-branch>/<workflow>/<artifact>\n```\n\nUse the exact short work-branch name and preserve `/` as path separators. For\nexample, artefacts for `feature/PAY-1234` live under\n`.agent-artifacts/feature/PAY-1234/`. A PR-scoped workflow uses the PR head\nbranch; a working-tree workflow uses the active branch. When no named branch can\nbe resolved for a revision-bound operation, use\n`.agent-artifacts/detached/<full-head-sha>/...`.\n\nRevision-sensitive workflows should add a revision directory beneath the\nworkflow when one is available, for example:\n\n```text\n.agent-artifacts/feature/PAY-1234/review/<head-sha>/report.md\n.agent-artifacts/feature/PAY-1234/review/<head-sha>/risk-map.json\n.agent-artifacts/feature/PAY-1234/implement/<commit-sha>/implementation-evidence.json\n.agent-artifacts/feature/PAY-1234/create-pr/<head-sha>/body.md\n```\n\nFor an uncommitted working-tree review, use a clearly non-revision label such as\n`review/working-tree/` and bind the artefact content to the reviewed base plus\nworking-tree evidence or digest.\n\nThis root is intentionally suitable for a single `.gitignore` entry. Before\nwriting repository-local supporting artefacts, verify the root is ignored and\ncontains no tracked files. Never add or modify ignore rules implicitly. If the\ncanonical root is not safely ignored, return the artefact inline or keep it in\norchestration state when possible; if an on-disk artefact is required to\ncontinue, stop with the missing storage prerequisite rather than writing to an\narbitrary repository path or external temporary directory.\n\nThe convention applies to workflow-supporting outputs such as review reports,\nrisk maps, implementation-evidence packets, resumable checkpoints, generated\nhandoffs, and temporary PR bodies. It does not relocate user-requested product\nor repository deliverables that are meant to be tracked as part of the change.\n\n## Public and internal skills\n\nPublic skills may be invoked directly. Workflow-internal modules sit behind an\nagent interface and fail closed without the owning agent's orchestration state.\n\nInternal modules use canonical metadata such as:\n\n```yaml\nmetadata:\n  mhingston.internal: \"true\"\n  mhingston.owner-agent: \"pr-review\"\n  mhingston.user-invocable: \"false\"\n```\n\nThis metadata communicates intent but is not an authorization boundary. The\nmodule's body must still require its owning agent's exact context and return\n`REQUIRED_ORCHESTRATOR_CONTEXT` when invoked directly. A runtime adapter may map\nthe metadata to its native visibility mechanism.\n\n## Agent catalogue\n\n| Agent | Use it for |\n| --- | --- |\n| [`implement`](agents/implement.md) | Orchestrate a ready ticket through a ticket-keyed feature branch, delegated behaviour-first implementation with falsifiable verification, independent technical review, explicit contract reconciliation, full build/test gates, and pull-request creation. |\n| [`pr-review`](agents/pr-review.md) | Require a current independent technical review and revision-bound risk map, provide proportionate comprehension support, redirect unresolved architecture decisions upstream, prepare explicit human judgement, and record the human verdict without approving or merging. |\n| [`refine`](agents/refine.md) | Classify selected work, clarify unresolved decisions, refine one bounded ticket or split larger clear work into agent-ready vertical slices, resolve publication targets, and update the selected tracker after human approval. |\n\n## Suggested workflows\n\nThe catalogue is composable rather than one mandatory SDLC. Start with the\nsmallest workflow that owns the outcome; add adjacent skills only when their\nextra evidence or control is useful. Square brackets below indicate optional\nstages rather than required ceremony.\n\n| Goal | Suggested flow | Notes |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Deliver a ticket | `refine` → [`plan`] → `implement` → [`pr-review`] | `plan` is useful when design or uncertainty deserves a separate non-mutating pass. `implement` already owns implementation, independent technical review, contract reconciliation, final project gates, and `create-pr`. Add `pr-review` when the formal human-verdict lifecycle is required. |\n| Isolate an unclear bug or regression | `fault-isolation` → [`plan`] → `implement` | Use `fault-isolation` when the causal mechanism is not established. Use `dynamic-workflows` when Mastra is specifically the executable runtime. |\n| Improve skills from experience | `wrap-up` → `session-lessons` → `skill-creator` | One run produces observations; longitudinal evidence qualifies durable changes; `skill-creator` evaluates proposed revisions.
